<role>
    You are a general-purpose analysis and coding agent.
</role>

<workflow>
    <constraints>
        - Do not fabricate data, sources, tool results, citations, or completed work.
        - When you use web sources, save a full BibTeX entry for each one with `e14c.web.cite_doi`, or `e14c.web.save_citation` when there is no DOI. The `citation-integrity` skill shows how.
        - Report limitations clearly, but stop only when you are confident the request cannot be completed.
        - Send all responses as tool calls.
    </constraints>
    <task-context>
        You were invoked either directly by a user or by an orchestrator as a sub-agent.
    </task-context>
    <protocol>
      1. Inspect the task, available files, and data before choosing an approach.
      2. For complex tasks, form a concise analysis plan. For simple tasks, proceed directly.
      3. Execute the work in the notebook.
      4. Write `.deliverables.json` in the working directory listing every file the answer reports. The file is `{"files": [{"path": "<absolute path, or a path relative to the working directory>", "description": "<what the file shows>", "kind": "final"}]}`. `kind` is `"final"` for the results the answer presents and `"intermediate"` for supporting artifacts. When the task finishes the platform uploads the `"final"` files, replaces their paths in your answer with `data_entry:` links, and hands those links to the caller; `"intermediate"` files stay in the workspace for sibling agents. At least one listed file must be `"final"`, even when the task says not to publish files or that the caller will upload them. Refer to each final file in the answer by the same path you listed. Do not call `e14c.data_storage.upload()` yourself, even when the task asks for an upload or a URI. The manifest is bookkeeping: do not list it, copy it into output folders, or mention it or the upload in the answer.
      5. Call `submit_answer` when the success criteria are satisfied.
    </protocol>
    <success-criteria>
      - The task is answered with verifiable evidence from executed notebook results.
      - Data issues, assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations are reported.
      - Report and briefly justify discretionary analytical decisions: choices between valid approaches where researchers could differ.
    </success-criteria>
    <environment>
      - The workspace has Jupyter notebook for Python analysis. R is available through `%%Rscript`.
      - You share the workspace with any orchestrator and sibling agents involved in the task. Follow task instructions for input and output locations, and organize generated files in folders.
      - `PERSONA_ID` and `PROJECT_ID` are available as environment variables.
      - If the task context is incomplete, inspect `memory/*_memory_*.jsonl` for relevant conversation history.

      You are operating in a production execution environment with internet access and tools for data analysis, API calls, and data retrieval.

      You do not have access to GPUs or specialized hardware.

      Execution time budgets:
      Each user message includes `cell_execution_time` and `total_execution_time` (seconds) as `<message-metadata>` attributes. The first limits one code cell. The latter is the total time available to respond to that user message and resets whenever the user sends a new message. You will receive warnings when you approach the `total_execution_time` limit.

      Execution resource limits:
      - cpu limit: 7
      - memory limit: 23Gi
      - /workspace directory limit: 50Gi
      - /tmp directory limit: 15Gi
      Plan execution around these limits. For large file operations, estimate peak disk usage first, including input, output, and temporary files. For memory-heavy work, estimate peak memory usage and use streaming or chunking when needed. If a plan may exceed a limit, use a smaller plan. The memory budget applies to the Python kernel and all subprocesses it starts, combined. Never raise, disable, or bypass these limits. After an allocation failure, do not move the same allocation into a subprocess, background job, or worker pool to work around it. Retry only after reducing peak memory usage enough to fit the existing budget. If that is not possible, stop the computation and explain the limitation. If you exceed the memory limit or a listed directory limit, execution will be stopped and work will be lost. Trust the limits above over measurements: `os.cpu_count()` sees visible cores rather than your cpu quota, available-memory figures are static, and `shutil.disk_usage`/`statvfs` may report the backing filesystem rather than your quota. Use `du -s <path>` to measure actual usage.
    </environment>
    <jupyter-notebook>
      - Use Python notebook cells by default. Run R code with the `%%Rscript` cell magic.
      - Exchange tabular data between Python and R using Parquet files.
      - R plots are not captured automatically; save them to a file and display the file from Python.
      - Edit and rerun failed cells instead of creating replacement cells.
      - Ensure every cell executes successfully. Do not create Markdown cells.
    </jupyter-notebook>

</workflow>

<output>
    <tone>
        Be direct, helpful and respectful. Be candid about disagreement and uncertainty. Omit generic praise and unnecessary sign-offs.
    </tone>
    <writing-style>
        Write in first person and present the work as yours. Use plain, simple and specific language. Define unfamiliar acronyms on the first use.

Reasonable default rcParams are set for matplotlib for fonts, grids, and colors. Ensure figures appear in both the notebook and to a file with higher DPI.

## Submodules
- `e14c.chemistry`: Design new molecules, predict chemical properties, and more.
- `e14c.citations`: Bibliography and gathered-evidence files saved on the workspace.
- `e14c.controlled_tools`: Call the pod-local controlled-tools service.
- `e14c.data_retrieval`: Search biological databases (Ensembl, GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, etc.).
- `e14c.data_storage`: Data Storage Service tools for uploading, tagging, and hosting artifacts. See e14c.edison_client for more granular control (incl permissions).
- `e14c.edison_client`: Public Edison client factory for agent-facing code.
- `e14c.filesystem`: Filesystem tools for writing and editing files.
- `e14c.image_generation`: Image generation using remote models.
- `e14c.path_sandbox`: Path sandbox for agent filesystem tools.
- `e14c.projects`
- `e14c.read`: Read PDFs, notebooks, DOCX, and PPTX into text and images.
- `e14c.reports`: Report generation and LaTeX template tools.
- `e14c.sirna`: Design and evaluate small interfering RNA (siRNA) drug candidates.
- `e14c.subagent_config`: Shared default job routing for platform subagents.
- `e14c.subagents`: Tools for dispatching sub-agent tasks via Edison platform.
- `e14c.web`: Scraping, web search, social media search, and web-source citation functions.

## Skill: subagents

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/subagents

Enabled `agent_type` values in this deployment:

- `"data-retrieval"`

## Overview

- You and the subagents share the same `/workspace`.
- Subagents have access to specialized tools and more compute resources.
- If available, `wait_for_subagents` will pause until one subagent finishes.
- `check_task` returns `TaskSummary` object with `status` (pending, success, etc) and `answer` (populated when task status is success).
- Use `PROJECT_ID` env variable for submitting tasks.

## Passing input files

- If the file is in the workspace, reference the absolute path.
- Do not upload that file to data storage for the handoff.
- Otherwise use `data_storage_uris`.

## Limits

Only 10 tasks can run concurrently.

## Sub-agent functionality

### Data retrieval

The `data-retrieval` sub-agent is a specialized system for retrieving data from a range of biological databases spanning expression, variants, structures, proteomics, pharmacology, and general data deposits e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, PRIDE, KEGG, Zenodo, among others and can also search sources beyond that set.

## Available Skills

Use `load_skill` to read a skill's guide before using it. Only load skills relevant to your current task.

- **base_chemistry**: Foundational chemistry workflow rules — SMILES handling, molecule validation, retrosynthesis and reaction prediction protocols, visualization, image recognition, and novelty detection. Shared by medicinal_chemistry and computational_chemistry.
- **bibliography**: Build one bibliography from literature tasks and saved literature and web citation files, and cite it in any deliverable format (LaTeX, Word, slides, HTML, spreadsheets).
- **citation-integrity**: Cite primary sources with full BibTeX, and save BibTeX for web sources with cite_doi or by hand.
- **computational_chemistry**: Used for computational chemistry tasks such as structure optimization, pka prediction, docking, co-folding, etc. via the Rowan API.
- **data-retrieval**: Retrieve data from common biological databases.
- **docx**: Use this skill when you need to *edit* or *create* a .docx file. It will help you inspect the structure of an existing docx, make edits to a docx, or create a new docx. Only load this skill if specifically directed to work with a .docx file. If not, prefer to write PDFs as directed by the `scientific-writing` skill.
- **genomics-nomenclature**: Use this when a task gives you a gene or variant whose name you need to normalize or expand before using it downstream. It shows how to resolve every synonymous name (aliases, previous/withdrawn symbols, loci, rsIDs, HGVS c./p./g., legacy and assembly-specific forms) from an authority, so downstream steps don't silently miss records filed under a former name.
- **html**: Writing a single HTML page to show in the conversation or share as a link. Covers the size it renders at, the light/dark handshake, and the palette and type to match the platform. Load when the deliverable is an HTML page.
- **medicinal_chemistry**: Reference guide for medicinal chemistry tasks, including drug metabolism, biotransformation, structural alerts, CYP polymorphism, bioisosteric replacements, and multi-parameter optimization.

# Who funds open-source-minded ventures? Scope and method (issue #380, round 2, part 3)

Sterling asked (PR #386, 2026-11-26): *"compile a list of investors, firms, philanthropists, and other VC and VC-like
sources that have been involved in funding a venture that falls into the more open-source minded of startups. Be
thorough and manual."* This file fixes the scope and the counting rules before any funding data is collected, so
that the list is not shaped by what turns up.

## What counts as an open-source-minded venture

A company (or a venture-like project that took outside money) whose main product is something it created or leads
and releases openly:

| Kind | Test |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial open source (COSS) | Its main paid product is an open-source project it leads, in another form: hosted service, open core, enterprise edition, licences, support. Projects later relicensed to source-available or fair-code licences stay in, flagged |
| Open-weight AI | Releases the weights of its main models for download (any licence; non-commercial licences flagged) |
| Open hardware | Publishes the design files of its main products under an open licence, or did so when it raised money |
| Open science | Its business is open-access publishing, open data, open protocols or open research tooling, even where its own code is closed (flagged) |
| Open-source platforms | Businesses whose product exists to host, fund or secure open source (GitHub, Tidelift, npm) — flagged; counted separately |

Corporate labs (Meta, Google, Microsoft) are not ventures and are out. Nonprofits are out of the deal list but their
funders are in the program list below.

## The ventures (three universes, each kept separate in the data)

- **U1, the systematic sample.** All 392 `core` companies from part 2's GitHub harvest (the 2,000 most-starred repos
  and the top 100 in each of 22 science topics; `../owners/data/finance_passes/input_all.csv`). Nobody picked these
  for their funding; they are in because their projects are popular on GitHub. Their classification was frozen in
  `efd5a76`, before this question was asked.
- **U2, open hardware, open science and science software.** Hand-picked: the first round's open hardware, lab and
  science companies (`../edison/inv_redteam_round1_files/ic_review/companies_analysis.csv`), plus open robotics,
  open instruments, lab automation, open-science publishing and tools, DeSci. Chosen for relevance to DAL and the
  SDL kit, so it is not a random sample.
- **U3, notable COSS and open-weight AI ventures not in U1.** The open-source listings from the H1 cohort
  (`../data/cohort_listings_verified.csv`), the first round's for-profit open-source companies, and well-known COSS
  exits, failures and AI labs from 1998 on. Chosen because they are known, which over-represents successes.

Every venture carries `universe` and `source_list` columns, so any count can be restricted to U1.

## What counts as a funder

Anyone who put money in, named in a public source: lead and participating investors in equity rounds, angels,
accelerators, corporate and strategic investors, crowdfunding (reward and equity), token sales (flagged),
philanthropic and government grants and prizes, venture debt where named. Acquirers and IPO buyers are not funders.
"Existing investors" without names are not counted.

Separately, a **program list** records philanthropic, government, corporate, crypto and community programs that fund
open source or open science at the program level (who, what program, years, amount, what it funds, whether it
funds companies), because much of that money goes to projects and nonprofits rather than to ventures.

## Counting rules

- One venture counts once per investor however many rounds the investor joined; rounds and leads are counted too.
- Investor names are normalised by an alias table kept in `data/investor_aliases.csv` (e.g. a16z = Andreessen
  Horowitz; GV = Google Ventures). Fund vehicles roll up to the firm. People are kept separate from their firms.
- Investor type is assigned centrally, by hand, after collection: venture firm, corporate venture or strategic,
  angel or person, accelerator or incubator, growth/PE/hedge/crossover, sovereign or public investor, philanthropy,
  government grant, crowdfunding, crypto fund or DAO, bank or debt, other.
- Every round needs a URL that states the investors or the amount. Database pages (Crunchbase, Tracxn, PitchBook
  profiles) are allowed but marked, and counted separately in a sensitivity check.
- Absence is recorded: a venture with no disclosed outside funding gets a row saying so.

## What the list cannot show

Disclosure is selective: big rounds and successful companies are reported more; small angels and failed companies
are not. U2 and U3 are hand-picked. A count of open-source deals says what an investor has done, not whether it

# Who funds open-source-minded ventures? (issue #380, round 2, part 3)

Sterling asked for *"a list of investors, firms, philanthropists, and other VC and VC-like sources that have been
involved in funding a venture that falls into the more open-source minded of startups. Be thorough and manual."*
This folder is that list.

- **[`FUNDER_LIST.md`](FUNDER_LIST.md) lists every funder found**, grouped by type, with each venture it backed
  linked to a page that names it.
- **This file** summarises the list, says what it shows and how far to trust it.
- **[`data/`](data/) holds the tables**:
  - every round (`deals.csv`)
  - every funder–venture pair (`investor_links.csv`)
  - every funder (`investors.csv`)
  - every program-level funder (`programs.csv`)

The scope and counting rules were committed before any funding data was gathered ([`PROTOCOL.md`](PROTOCOL.md),
`448c8c2`).

## Bottom line

- **The list is long and flat.** Across the 640 hand-researched ventures in groups U1–U3,
  448 disclosed outside funding.
  - Public sources name 1,697 distinct funders in 1,320 funding events.
  - 1,294 of those funders appear in only one venture.
  - Only 102 backed five or more, and the ten most frequent account for
    9% of all funder–venture links.
  - There is no small club that funds open source. There is a long tail with a recognisable head.
- **The head is mostly generalist venture firms, an accelerator and chip and cloud companies:**
  - Y Combinator, by count.
  - Accel, Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Index, Benchmark, Lightspeed and Insight.
  - Corporate investors, counted across all four groups with their arms rolled up to the parent:
    - Alphabet: GV, CapitalG, Gradient and Google together, 44 ventures
    - Intel Capital (24) and NVIDIA (22)
    - Microsoft: M12, GitHub and Microsoft, 20
    - Samsung (20) and Salesforce Ventures (19)
  - The firms that lead open-source rounds most often are Andreessen Horowitz, Accel, Insight, NEA, Sequoia,
    Index and Benchmark.
- **Funds built around open source exist, but most are small in this count.**
  - The exceptions are OSS Capital, with 15 ventures across all four groups, and Uncorrelated
    Ventures, with 14. For comparison, Bessemer has 20 and
    GV 20.
  - Runa Capital (5), Heavybit (5), Boldstart (4),
    Crane (4) and Open Core Ventures (4) back only a handful
    each.
  - 26 funders in the data state an open-source thesis in their own words. Most of them are large
    generalists: Andreessen Horowitz, Accel, Sequoia, Index, NEA and Redpoint.
- **People are a large share of the funders.** Many of the most frequent angels founded or led open-source
  companies themselves, and now back the next ones (ventures here, all groups):
  - Guillermo Rauch of Vercel (20), Clem Delangue of Hugging Face (9) and
    David Cramer of Sentry (10)
  - Tom Preston-Werner (10) and Nat Friedman (9) of GitHub, Paul
    Copplestone of Supabase (9) and Tristan Handy of dbt Labs (5)
- **Open hardware, open science and lab ventures draw a different mix**: crowdfunding backers, strategic
  corporates, a few hardware-minded venture firms, grants and, for DeSci, crypto funds.
  - Strategic corporates: Bosch, Renesas, Arm, Qualcomm, Sony, Intel and NVIDIA.
  - Hardware-minded venture firms: True Ventures, Foundry Group, Spark Capital, Khosla, Eclipse and Lux.
  - Grants: SBIR, NSF, NIH, Shuttleworth, CZI and Sloan.
  - Only 13 funders backed three or more of the 97 ventures in this group.
- **Philanthropy and government fund open source mostly at the program level**, and mostly not through companies.
  - Programs: CZI, Sloan, Moore and Schmidt Sciences; DOE's Exascale Computing Project; NSF's POSE and CSSI;
    Germany's Sovereign Tech Agency; the EU's NGI grants through NLnet.
  - Recipients are mostly projects, universities and nonprofits.
- **The list is accurate but incomplete. Treat every count as a lower bound.**
  - 94% of the investor names checked appear on the page their round cites.
  - Edison's blind audit of 40 random ventures found 86% of this list's names
    for those ventures. It also found about 296 funders where this list has
    180, mostly smaller participants, angels, grants and lenders.
- **Nothing here says these funders made money on open source, or that they would fund a given venture.** The list
  records who put money in, as disclosed. Disclosure favours large rounds and survivors.

![Who has backed the most open-source-minded ventures](figures/top_funders.png)

## The funders that backed the most open-source-minded ventures (U1–U3)

One count per venture, however many rounds; "led" counts ventures where the funder led at least one round.
Examples list led ventures first. Full list: [`FUNDER_LIST.md`](FUNDER_LIST.md).

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Y Combinator | accelerator / studio | 60 | 3 | Mattermost, PostHog Inc., SigNoz, Activepieces, Airbyte, Anomaly, 
<...output truncated to 10000 characters (edit the cell to produce a shorter output if needed)...>
sses found little that was new, a sign that these sources were exhausted.
   - A separate check confirmed 24 investor–venture links from investors' own portfolio pages; it rejected 2.
6. **Program passes.** Six passes listed the programs that fund open source and open science outside equity
   rounds: foundations (twice, the second through the Moore and Sloan grants databases), governments and public
   investors, corporate funds, crypto, accelerators, fellowships and crowdfunding. They also recorded investors
   that state an open-source thesis, in their own words.
7. **Merge.** `scripts/build_funders.py` normalises names with a hand-made alias table
   ([`data/investor_aliases.csv`](data/investor_aliases.csv)) and types each funder from a hand-made table
   ([`data/investor_types.csv`](data/investor_types.csv), by the firm's own description; people count as angels).
   - A round that a source reports only as talks, a rumour or a raise in progress is kept, but its names are not
     counted (`counted` column in `deals.csv`).
   - Claude Opus planned the passes, wrote the scripts, reviewed the rows and wrote this file.

## Limits

- **Disclosure is selective.** Big rounds, well-known investors and companies that survived are reported more.
  Seed angels, small funds, failures and private companies outside the US and Europe are reported less. Counts
  therefore favour large, visible firms.
- **Coverage is uneven.** The search budget ran out early, so many ventures were researched only from news APIs,
  Wikipedia and company pages.
  - Web search was available only for the program passes, all five U2 passes, three U3 passes and about four
    U1 passes; the rest relied on the open APIs and direct fetches.
  - Chinese-language sources were read for a handful of companies only.
  - U4 (young startups) was researched lightly by design: for most of it, YC's own page and a quick look at the
    company site.
- **"None found" means none found.** Of the companies behind the most-starred projects, 147 have no
  disclosed outside funding in this data. Some will have raised money that was never announced or that these
  sources don't reach.
- **U2, U3 and U4 are not random.** U2 was picked for relevance and U3 for fame. U4 comes from lists kept by an
  accelerator (YC) and an investor (Runa), which both have an interest in the companies on them.
- **A count is not a return.** Nothing here measures whether these funders made money on open source. Edison found
  no study that does. Being on the list doesn't mean a funder would back a new open venture.
- **Names are normalised by hand.** Fund vehicles roll up to the firm, and corporate arms stay separate but roll up
  to their parent in one table. Some aliases will be missed, and a few distinct firms share a name.
- **Rounds are as sources describe them.** Labels (seed, Series A) and amounts follow the source, and sources
  sometimes disagree; the rows say so in `note`.

message.content:
Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/citation-integrity

- Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or a subagent task.
- Every primary source needs a full BibTeX entry. Cite from the BibTeX, not from a narrative answer.
- Never cite yourself or guess citations from memory.

## Web sources

Every source you use from the `e14c.web` tools needs a full BibTeX entry.

- When you write an entry yourself, name its key with the first author's surname, the year, and the first word of the title, for example `jumper2021highly`. This keeps keys unique.
- Save each entry with `e14c.web.save_citation(bibtex)` as soon as you use the source. It appends the entry to your own file in the project's citations folder, `$WORKSPACE_PATH/citations/$PROJECT_ID/$TRAJECTORY_ID.bib`. In a chat session, `TRAJECTORY_ID` is the session ID. Do not write citation files any other way.

### Sources with a DOI

Call `await e14c.web.cite_doi(doi)`. It fetches the BibTeX from doi.org and saves it. This works for Crossref and DataCite DOIs, including arXiv DOIs such as `10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762`. Check that the title and authors in the returned entry match the paper you read.

### Sources without a DOI

Write the BibTeX entry yourself. Take every field from the source, never from memory.

- Use `@online` for web pages, database records, datasets, software, and reports. The report template hides URLs for most entry types, but it always prints them for `@online`, so readers can find the source.
- Include `author`, `title`, `url`, and `urldate`. `urldate` is the date you accessed the page, written as `YYYY-MM-DD`. Add `date` when the page shows a publication or update date.
- When there is no personal author, put the organization in `author` inside double braces, such as `{{UniProt Consortium}}`. The double braces stop it from being split into first and last names. Use the organization's short name in the key.
- When the page has no date, use the access year in the key.
- Many scholarly pages list their title, authors, and date in `citation_*` meta tags. `(await e14c.web.fetch_page(url)).text` returns the raw HTML so you can read them.
- In `title`, escape `&`, `%`, `_`, and `#` with a backslash, and wrap acronyms in braces to keep their capitals. Do not escape anything in `url`.
- For a journal article with no DOI, use `@article` with `journal`, `volume`, `number`, `pages`, and `year` instead. These fields let a reader find it without a link.

```bibtex
@online{uniprot2026uniprotkb,
  author  = {{UniProt Consortium}},
  title   = {{UniProtKB} entry {P04637} ({P53\_HUMAN}): Cellular tumor antigen p53},
  url     = {https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04637/entry},
  urldate = {2026-10-12},
}
```

# Who funds open-source-minded ventures? Scope and method (issue #380, round 2, part 3)

Sterling asked (PR #386, 2026-11-26): *"compile a list of investors, firms, philanthropists, and other VC and VC-like
sources that have been involved in funding a venture that falls into the more open-source minded of startups. Be
thorough and manual."* This file fixes the scope and the counting rules before any funding data is collected, so
that the list is not shaped by what turns up.

## What counts as an open-source-minded venture

A company (or a venture-like project that took outside money) whose main product is something it created or leads
and releases openly:

| Kind | Test |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial open source (COSS) | Its main paid product is an open-source project it leads, in another form: hosted service, open core, enterprise edition, licences, support. Projects later relicensed to source-available or fair-code licences stay in, flagged |
| Open-weight AI | Releases the weights of its main models for download (any licence; non-commercial licences flagged) |
| Open hardware | Publishes the design files of its main products under an open licence, or did so when it raised money |
| Open science | Its business is open-access publishing, open data, open protocols or open research tooling, even where its own code is closed (flagged) |
| Open-source platforms | Businesses whose product exists to host, fund or secure open source (GitHub, Tidelift, npm) — flagged; counted separately |

Corporate labs (Meta, Google, Microsoft) are not ventures and are out. Nonprofits are out of the deal list but their
funders are in the program list below.

## The ventures (three universes, each kept separate in the data)

- **U1, the systematic sample.** All 392 `core` companies from part 2's GitHub harvest (the 2,000 most-starred repos
  and the top 100 in each of 22 science topics; `../owners/data/finance_passes/input_all.csv`). Nobody picked these
  for their funding; they are in because their projects are popular on GitHub. Their classification was frozen in
  `efd5a76`, before this question was asked.
- **U2, open hardware, open science and science software.** Hand-picked: the first round's open hardware, lab and
  science companies (`../edison/inv_redteam_round1_files/ic_review/companies_analysis.csv`), plus open robotics,
  open instruments, lab automation, open-science publishing and tools, DeSci. Chosen for relevance to DAL and the
  SDL kit, so it is not a random sample.
- **U3, notable COSS and open-weight AI ventures not in U1.** The open-source listings from the H1 cohort
  (`../data/cohort_listings_verified.csv`), the first round's for-profit open-source companies, and well-known COSS
  exits, failures and AI labs from 1998 on. Chosen because they are known, which over-represents successes.

Every venture carries `universe` and `source_list` columns, so any count can be restricted to U1.

## What counts as a funder

Anyone who put money in, named in a public source: lead and participating investors in equity rounds, angels,
accelerators, corporate and strategic investors, crowdfunding (reward and equity), token sales (flagged),
philanthropic and government grants and prizes, venture debt where named. Acquirers and IPO buyers are not funders.
"Existing investors" without names are not counted.

Separately, a **program list** records philanthropic, government, corporate, crypto and community programs that fund
open source or open science at the program level (who, what program, years, amount, what it funds, whether it
funds companies), because much of that money goes to projects and nonprofits rather than to ventures.

## Counting rules

- One venture counts once per investor however many rounds the investor joined; rounds and leads are counted too.
- Investor names are normalised by an alias table kept in `data/investor_aliases.csv` (e.g. a16z = Andreessen
  Horowitz; GV = Google Ventures). Fund vehicles roll up to the firm. People are kept separate from their firms.
- Investor type is assigned centrally, by hand, after collection: venture firm, corporate venture or strategic,
  angel or person, accelerator or incubator, growth/PE/hedge/crossover, sovereign or public investor, philanthropy,
  government grant, crowdfunding, crypto fund or DAO, bank or debt, other.
- Every round needs a URL that states the investors or the amount. Database pages (Crunchbase, Tracxn, PitchBook
  profiles) are allowed but marked, and counted separately in a sensitivity check.
- Absence is recorded: a venture with no disclosed outside funding gets a row saying so.

## What the list cannot show

Disclosure is selective: big rounds and successful companies are reported more; small angels and failed companies
are not. U2 and U3 are hand-picked. A count of open-source deals says what an investor has done, not whether it
made money or will do it again, and nothing here is advice to approach anyone.

async def web_search(query: str, *, category: SearchCategory | None = None, include_domains: list[str] | None = None, exclude_domains: list[str] | None = None, num_results: int = 10) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Search the web and return results with text and highlights.

    Each result includes full page text (Markdown, capped at
    5,000 chars) and a highlight snippet.

    Args:
        query: Natural language search query.
        category: Optional filter — ``company``, ``people``,
            ``scholarly``, ``news``, or ``financial``.
        include_domains: Restrict results to these domains.
        exclude_domains: Exclude results from these domains.
        num_results: Number of results (default 10, capped at 100).

    Returns:
        A list of dicts with keys: ``title``, ``url``,
        ``publishedDate``, ``full_text``, ``snippet``, ``links``.
    """
```

    Returns:

    """
```

**e14c.web.save_citation**
```python
def save_citation(bibtex: str) -> Path:
    """
    Append a BibTeX entry for a web source to this agent's citations file.

    Each agent writes only to
    ``$WORKSPACE_PATH/citations/$PROJECT_ID/$TRAJECTORY_ID.bib``, so agents
    running in parallel never share a file. In chat sessions heron sets
    ``TRAJECTORY_ID`` to the session ID, so an orchestrator keeps one file
    across turns. ``e14c.citations.citation_files`` lists the ``.bib`` files
    in that directory.

    Example:
        save_citation(bibtex)  # from doi.org, or written by hand

    Returns:
        The path of the file the entry was appended to.
    """
```

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/scientific-writing

# Scientific Writing

A report PDF is produced by compiling the Edison LaTeX template.

## 1. LaTeX setup

First, create a clean latex working directory, such as `latex_report/`.

Then, make two calls to fetch template latex files and build a bibliography.

### Download template files

```python
from e14c.reports.latex import fetch_edison_template

fetch_edison_template("latex_report")
```

This places the following in `latex_report/`:

- `template.tex` - loads arxiv package, additional default Edison styles, and document structure. Rename this to something more descriptive
- `arxiv.sty`
- `references.bib` - placeholder
- `edison-logo.pdf` - logo for the cover page (already configured in the template)

### House style lock

`template.tex` is a complete report with the house style already wired in - cover page, logo, colour palette, callout boxes, and the Data Sources table. Rename it, then fill it in: replace the `[REPLACE]` placeholders with your content and leave the `[KEEP]` blocks alone.

Compile that renamed copy as is - the preamble stays as fetched, the `[KEEP]` blocks stay where they are, and `arxiv.sty` is never edited. Fill the `[REPLACE]` placeholders and add sections between them; do not rebuild the document body around a cover page of your own. Depart from the house style only when the task explicitly says not to use the Edison template; adjectives like polished or demo-quality are not an opt-out.

If compile errors are in your content, fix the content. If they are in the template or `arxiv.sty`, report them; do not replace the template to get a clean compile.

### Build the bibliography

Build `latex_report/references.bib` as described in the `bibliography` skill. Load that skill first if it is not already loaded. It merges the literature task citations and the saved literature and web citation files into one file. The template's `\printbibliography` renders it.

Note: this overwrites anything in `references.bib`.

## 2. Drafting

### Skeleton

The orchestrator agent may have provided an outline of structural elements for the main text. Try to adhere to those. If the outline is ambiguous, here is an example

```
 1. Cover page
 2. Abstract / Executive Summary: one page max.
 3. Table of contents: long reports only (>= 10 pages). Omit for shorter reports.
 4. Introduction / Context: what is known, what the gap is.
 5. Methodology: reference trajectory/tasks as needed.
 6. Main content sections: organized by research question
 7. Recommendations (if needed): tiered near-, medium-, long-term
 8. Discussion / Caveats / Limitations: standalone or per-recommendation
 9. Conclusion: brief synthesis
10. Output provenance table: every asset to a real task UUID with a chat_url link
11. Bibliography: generated from references.bib via biblatex
```

## 3. Paper elements

Read the fetched template before drafting and reuse its approved patterns.

### Literature citations

Cite in-line using `\citep{key}`, or for multiple citations, `\citep{key1,key2}`. The template's `biblatex` (numbered style) handles rendering as `[N]` and truncates long author lists to the first 6 + "et al.".

The `template.tex` contains a command to render the bibliography.

### Edison trajectory citations

Any outputs of tasks (especially analyses tasks) that appear in the paper should be properly referenced to allow the reader to trace back to the originating trajectory. Ideal places to include these references include:

- The end of a figure/table legend
- Within a methods section
- Within a results section

Sub-agent outputs use the sub-agent's UUID, passed in via the dispatch. Outputs you produced yourself use `os.environ["TRAJECTORY_ID"]`. Never use `ORCHESTRATOR` or any placeholder string.

`\edtraj{<url>}{<short>}` renders `Edison: <short>` for inline trajectory references. Trajectory URLs should be obtained programmatically to reduce errors as follows:

```python
from e14c.subagents import chat_url

sub_url = chat_url("74d1ef6b-0f34-4805-ba2b-c110086e7e93")  # task (default)
self_url = chat_url()  # this trajectory
artifact_url = chat_url("report-pdf-ab12", kind="data_entry")  # uploaded artifact
```

For artifacts, wrap with href:

```latex
\href{<artifact_url>}{data\_entry:report-pdf-ab12}
```

See the template for how to update the Edison Platform Data Sources table.

### Tables and statistics

- Booktabs and alternating row shading on tables where it aids readability.
- Color-code priority programs.
- P-values appear alongside ORs/betas. No naked effect sizes. For discovery analyses, show only FDR-significant results.

### Figures

One overview figure per report.

- `e14c.image_generation.generate_image` for label-heavy scientific figures.
- `e14c.image_generation.generate_infographic` for non-text-heavy conceptual overviews.

You may also pass a reference image to edit.

Visual style: white or light background, muted palette (navy/black/gray), Nature-style, publication-ready. No chartjunk, no cartoon styling, no decoration. Every figure caption ends with the producing task UUID, hyperlinked via `chat_url` (see Edison trajectory citations above).

## 4. Pre-delivery validation

Complete the applicable checks before calling `submit_answer`.

### Build

- [ ] Compile the actual main `.tex` file with `tectonic`. Resolve compilation errors, undefined references, and alignment errors.
- [ ] Unless the task opted out of the house style, confirm the compiled file is the renamed template: the preamble differs from the fetched `template.tex` only by `[REPLACE]` substitutions, the `[KEEP]` blocks and the template cover page are intact, and `arxiv.sty` is unchanged. A hand-written preamble that loads `arxiv`, or a self-authored `titlepage` in place of the template cover, does not qualify.
- [ ] Confirm every `\citep{key}` resolves to an entry in `references.bib`.
- [ ] Include a table of contents only when the final PDF is at least 10 pages.
- [ ] Place `\FloatBarrier` or `\clearpage` before References so figures and tables cannot drift beyond it.

### Content and provenance

- [ ] Check every quantitative claim against the originating task output.
- [ ] Sweep the draft for claims with no citation. For each, either attach the source or restate it as explicit inference.
- [ ] Confirm figure and table captions, numbering, and in-text references agree.
- [ ] Ensure repeated values, ranked lists, scores, and entity sets are consistent across sections.
- [ ] Associate every task-derived asset with its originating task UUID and `chat_url`.
- [ ] Wrap artifact references using `chat_url(<id>, kind="data_entry")`.
- [ ] Upload every supporting file named for the reader and reference it with a `data_entry:` URI.
- [ ] Remove placeholders, draft or version labels, prior-iteration language, and inaccessible internal paths.
- [ ] Remove meta-context, including mentions of prompts, system internals, the orchestrator, or the document-generation process.

### Layout

- [ ] For new documents or changes that can affect layout, use `explore` to inspect every rendered PDF page for overflowing tables, clipped figures, misplaced floats, orphaned headings, blank pages, and excessive whitespace.
- [ ] For a targeted layout fix, inspect the affected pages again. Skip full layout inspection only for minor text edits unlikely to change pagination.

Run each applicable check once. If one fails, fix the issue and rerun only the affected checks. Submit when all applicable checks pass.

 # Benchmarking LLM Agents on Scientific Tasks

Toward a rigorous, extensible framework for evaluating AI as a scientific collaborator

## Overview

As large language models (LLMs) rapidly advance, their potential to assist or even independently conduct scientific research has captured wide attention. From summarizing literature to generating code, LLMs already perform parts of the research process. Yet their credibility, validity, and replicability as scientific contributors remain largely untested. The Benchmarking LLM Agents on Scientific Tasks project, led by the Center for Open Science (COS) with support from Coefficient Giving, is a multi-year, multi-team initiative to systematically evaluate how well LLM agents can perform and reason through the scientific research lifecycle.

## A Multi-Persona Framework for AI in Science

The project defines a structured framework that benchmarks LLM agents according to three core researcher personas, each representing distinct capabilities and roles within the research ecosystem:

- Replicate (Replicator): The agent’s ability to replicate published studies using shared data, code, and new data to test whether original results hold.
- Evaluate (Peer Reviewer): The agent’s ability to critically evaluate completed research, identifying methodological strengths and weaknesses, assessing claims, and estimating replicability.
- Generate (Discovery Scientist): The agent’s ability to propose novel research questions, design studies, conduct analyses, and interpret findings with scientific rigor.

Each persona is mapped onto stages of the research lifecycle—design, conduct, analyze, and interpret—producing a scalable matrix of tasks that can be used to benchmark progress in increasingly complex and autonomous forms of scientific reasoni

### Factored Cognition

In our Factored Cognition project, we explore whether we can answer difficult questions by decomposing the cognitive work involved into small pieces that can be tackled by individual agents who don't know the big picture.

...

#### Implementation

Since March, we have implemented and open-sourced two prototypes, Mosaic and Patchwork.

Mosaic is a web app built by Ozzie Gooen and Andrew Schreiber that supports creating and editing recursive question-answer trees with pointers. It doesn't support automation, doesn't currently schedule work between multiple users, and still has a number of usability issues. You can take a look at our running instance or check out the source code.

Patchwork was built by Ben Weinstein-Raun and is a command-line app aimed at developing robust foundations for the next version of Mosaic, with principled support for multiple users and extensive automation. The repository includes a short screencast. Like Mosaic, it is a MIT-licensed open-source project.

...

## Organization and funding

The IRS approved our application for 501(c)(3) status, which means that donations are now tax-deductible. We're not actively seeking donations at the moment and are primarily talent-constrained.

The Open Philanthropy Project made a $525k grant to us. You can read their grant report.

function.arguments:
{"code": "report = r'''# Independent review of `FUNDERS.md`

**Scope of review, 26 November 2026.** I treated `PROTOCOL.md` as the precommitted inclusion rule and independently recomputed the claims from the seven supplied CSVs, without changing them. CSV row numbers below are physical file line numbers (header is line 1); Markdown line numbers refer to the supplied `FUNDERS.md`. My reproducible checks, including per-cell comparisons, are in [`review_support/audit_checks.csv`](review_support/audit_checks.csv) and [`review_support/recompute.py`](review_support/recompute.py). External primary-source URLs below are documented with full BibTeX in [`review_support/references.bib`](review_support/references.bib). I treat separate scope, alias, and transaction corrections as **sensitivities**, not as a fully reconstructed clean dataset.

## Ranked findings

### 1. Critical — acquisition proceeds, secondary sellers and an initial public offering are called venture funding

**Evidence.** `PROTOCOL.md`, “What counts as a funder,” explicitly excludes acquirers and initial-public-offering (IPO) buyers. Yet `deals.csv` rows **864** (KKR and Clayton, Dubilier & Rice's **$5.3 billion Cloudera buyout**), **898–902** (SUSE acquired by Novell for **$210 million**, sold to EQT for **$2.535 billion**, EQT take-private, Attachmate's **$2.2 billion Novell acquisition**, and SUSE IPO) and **933** (Thoma Bravo's **$2.3 billion ForgeRock acquisition**) all have `counted=yes`. Row **846** records the Red Hat IPO with `counted=yes`, albeit without a named buyer. Cloudera's own [announcement](https://www.cloudera.com/about/news-and-blogs/press-releases/2021-06-01-cloudera-enters-into-definitive-agreement-to-be-acquired-by-clayton-dubilier-and-rice-and-kkr-for-5-point-3-billion-dollars.html) explicitly calls $5.3 billion an *all-cash acquisition price*, not growth capital [`cloudera2021`]. `deals.csv` rows **202–203** list shareholders *selling* Odoo shares in secondary transactions as “investors”; those names must not be inferred to have invested in that transaction, even though they may have invested earlier. For just eight indisputable acquisition/IPO rows (846, 864, 898–902, 933), removing the deal-derived links eliminates **six unique funder–venture pairs** and changes **2,024 to 2,021** funders in U1–U4 (**1,697 to 1,694** in U1–U3). The complete amount contamination cannot be computed without adjudicating every sale and secondary transaction.

**Correction.** Split financing paid **to the venture** from ownership transfers, take-privates, shareholder sales and IPOs; move the latter to an exits/secondary table with `counted=no`. Recalculate funder and deal counts and prohibit summing buyout prices into funding totals. Keep original investor names only where an independently sourced *earlier* capital investment is documented. This matters more than a small rank change: a $5.3 billion buyout misrepresents the sort of cheque available to a new lab venture.

### 2. High — ventures and grants that the protocol excludes or cannot establish as open remain in the headline universe

**Evidence.** `PROTOCOL.md` excludes nonprofits from the **deal** list and requires the **main product** to pass an openness test. In `ventures.csv`, rows **846** (`u4-our-world-in-data`, five investor links) and **942** (`u4-votingworks`, 14 links) are nonprofits: their own [funding page](https://ourworldindata.org/funding) calls Our World in Data's publisher a registered charity [`owid2026`], and VotingWorks [calls itself a 501(c)(3) nonprofit](https://www.voting.works/about) [`votingworks2026`]. Row **657** (`u4-arc-prize-foundation`, one accelerator link) is also a foundation; its corporate form needs checking before treating that link as venture financing. These three rows account for **20 links**, without proving that every listed supporter is wrongly recorded as a donor. `ventures.csv` explicitly marks **six** U4 ventures `open_ok=no`; four funded ones—rows **650** Airtrain AI, **653** Alpaca (brokerage API, not an open main product), **680** Cakework and **882** Rownd—supply **15 more links** (`investor_links.csv` rows **46, 1,072, 1,165, 1,700, 2,492, 2,818, 3,023, 3,295, 3,330, 3,585, 3,651, 3,824, 3,827, 3,852, 4,048**). Non-U4 cases also warrant actual open-product checks: `ventures.csv` row **609**, Reflection AI, says no weights release had been confirmed yet (**14 investor links**); row **471**, Trilobio, describes the **lab-automation platform as closed**, with only API/tooling repositories open (**12 links**); rows **403** SiFive and **470** Tenstorrent say their principal chip designs are proprietary. An open instruction-set architecture or software *around* closed chips is not proof of openly licensed main-hardware design. U2 has **37/97** `open_ok=partial` entries.

**Correction.** Exclude explicit `open_ok=no` ventures, transfer nonprofit funders to `programs.csv`, and re-audit each `partial` row against the *main-product* test at the financing date. Publish strict and broad counts, with platforms and open-weight-but-closed-product cases separate. The U1–U3 headline is not directly changed by the U4 `no` rows, but U2 comparables and all-group/early-round advice are affected.

### 3. High — repeated company aliases inflate the U4 early-stage and angel rankings

**Evidence.** Identical company histories have been counted under separate U1/U4 keys: `ventures.csv` rows **77/977** (`mem0ai`/Embedchain), **205/973** (Onyx/Danswer), **256/1,011** (Reflex/Pynecone), **23/969** (Comfy Org/ComfyUI). In three pairs the two investor sets are **identical** (15, 6 and 13 names respectively); the Comfy names overlap in **4/6** each. Two more duplicate repo/company pairs appear at rows **957/960** (AITable/APITable; same `open_url`) and **1,041/1,042** (Zinc/ZincSearch; same `open_url`). Conservatively merging only these **six** identified pairs changes U1–U4 from **1,042 to 1,036 distinct ventures**, and funder–venture links from **4,178 to 4,136**; these are the same companies, not six additional financing opportunities. `investors.csv`/`investor_links.csv` then give **Y Combinator 310**, rather than **313**; **Paul Copplestone 7**, rather than **9**; **Guillermo Rauch 19**, rather than **20**. This does not disturb U1–U3-only rankings, but it directly changes the bottom-line people/accelerator examples (the bottom line uses all four groups).

**Correction.** Create a venture-entity alias table before deduplicating investor–venture pairs; assign one canonical key per company, allow name histories and subsidiaries as attributes, and separately label genuine successor companies. Recompute U4 and all-universe top-funder/early-round tables.

### 4. High — the “only 1,320 funding events” statement is not reproducible, while the other headline totals are

**Evidence.** `FUNDERS.md` line **23** claims **1,320 funding events** across the 640 U1–U3 ventures. In `deals.csv`, those universes contain **1,386 rows**, **1,381** with `counted=yes`; restricting to rows with a named funder yields **1,265**. Even an *approximate*, not validated, duplicate-event grouping by `(key, date, type, amount_usd)` yields **1,319 counted groups**, not 1,320. Different month labels, vague dates, inconsistent labels and extra investor lists make grouping by those four fields unreliable: for example, `deals.csv` rows **63, 64 and 66** repeat Grafana's August 2024 $270 million financing, while rows **62 and 65** cover its February 2022 $240 million financing. Identical rows **64/66** and **360/362** are exact duplicates. `ventures.csv.n_rounds` sums to **1,386** in U1–U3, matching *rows*, not unique financings. I cannot determine which events were intended to constitute **1,320** without the missing build/deduplication rule. The reported **1,697** distinct U1–U3 funders, **1,294** one-venture funders, **102** with at least five, and top-ten share of **291/3,137=9.28% (~9%)** are exactly reproducible from `investor_links.csv`.

**Correction.** Assign a reviewed `round_id` to each real financing, merge sources and investor lists into that event, explicitly mark uncertain/undated events and separately count named-funder and unnamed events. Either publish the resulting event count and its script or replace “1,320 funding events” with “1,381 counted deal **records**, including duplicates and non-financing records” pending repair.

### 5. High — the “accurate but incomplete; every count is a lower bound” claim overstates precision

**Evidence.** The source checker (`source_checks_deals.csv`) reports **4,815 `found`**, **164 `in page markup`**, **139 `not on page`** and **214 `unavailable`** out of **5,332 checked name occurrences**. `FUNDERS.md` line **586** correctly computes **4,815/5,118=94.08%** *text matches on fetchable pages*, or **4,979/5,118=97.28%** if markup matches count; neither measures whether the person or institution actually **invested**. Examples in `source_checks_deals.csv` rows **88–95** are Vercel investor names absent from its cited About page; row **133** flags a purported YC participant on the cited Nous Research page; others may have independent support. `investor_links.csv` flags **143/4,178** links as *database/Wikipedia-only*, and `FUNDERS.md` does not supply the protocol-promised source-quality sensitivity: omitting those flags yields **4,035 links / 1,968 funders**, versus **4,178 / 2,024** in U1–U4. That flag is narrower than “any link ever touched by Wikipedia”: it identifies links whose sources are *only* database/Wikipedia. Independently, Findings 1–3 demonstrate overcounting. The audit overlap measures incomplete recall **relative to another list**, not true positive predictive value. Moreover, `ventures.csv` shows **nine `funding_found=yes` ventures without a named link** and one `funding_found=none_found` venture with a link (ARC Prize Foundation). Therefore, *every count is a lower bound* is false for observed event, venture and funder counts: missing funders and spurious ones operate in opposite directions.

**Correction.** Say **“a disclosed, selectively researched inventory with both omissions and false inclusions; its raw counts are neither population estimates nor certified lower bounds.”** Report source quality by investor/link, validate roles in context, and publish separate strict-source, permissive-source and scope-corrected tables. Do not use the 94% string-match rate as a 94% investment-verification rate.

### 6. Medium-high — repeated funders, funder types and corporate-parent rollups remain insufficiently normalized

**Evidence.** `investors.csv` rows **38/120** record **Sapphire Ventures** as a venture firm with **13** ventures and **SAP Ventures** as corporate venture with **5**. Their own [2014 announcement](https://sapphireventures.com/press/sap-ventures-becomes-sapphire-ventures/) states SAP Ventures *became* Sapphire Ventures [`sapphire2014`]. A firm-level rollup across those names yields **17 distinct ventures** (one in common), which lifts it from the 13-venture tier; do not treat the independently operating post-2014 firm as SAP's current corporate arm. `investors.csv` rows **316/1,612** similarly split **Partech** (venture firm, 2) from **Partech International** (*government grant*, 1)—Partech describes itself as an independent venture investor, with a historical Paribas spinout [`partech2022`]. Other transparent case-only duplications include `System.One`/`System.one` (rows **508/1,840**), `Translink Capital`/`TransLink Capital` (**517/1,886**) and `ZhenFund`/`Zhenfund` (**525/2,014**). Merging just Sapphire/SAP, Partech/Partech International, plus seven exact case-variant pairs, takes U1–U3 **1,697 to 1,690** funders, singletons **1,294 to 1,284**, and funders with at least five ventures **102 to 101**; one overlapping Sapphire/SAP venture removes one U1–U3 link. Do **not** automatically roll up parent vs arm, similarly named firms or individuals without checking control and dates (e.g. `Fidelity` versus `Fidelity Ventures`). `investors.csv` also puts **Partech International** in `government_grant` and **National Social Security Fund Zhongguancun Fund (Legend Capital)** (row **640**) in `government_grant` despite being described as a fund; `Wells Fargo` (row **521**) is `unclassified` despite lender links in `deals.csv`. **1,197/2,024** investor-type assignments are `heuristic`, and **69** are still `unclassified` (**70 links**).

**Correction.** Apply a dated entity/vehicle hierarchy with per-row evidence, distinguish historical corporate ownership from current type, and review all high-count and grant/public-money categories manually. Recompute the long-tail/type mix with a disclosed alias table; the present head and tail are descriptive, not robustly normalized.

### 7. Medium-high — the physical-science section conflates a single crowdfunding label with a dominant funding channel

**Evidence.** The line “Crowdfunding is the most common single source” (`FUNDERS.md` lines **412–414**) is true **only as a single repeated investor label**: U2 has **Kickstarter backers on 13/97** ventures (the broader U1-science plus U2 table gives **14**, consistent with lines 370–389). At the **type** level, U2 has **178 venture-firm** links and **56 corporate/strategic** links, versus **24 crowdfunding** links; its crowdfunding links occur across **19/97** ventures versus **40/97** ventures with a venture firm and **29/97** with a corporate investor (`investor_links.csv` + `investors.csv`). Program-level support is a separate pool: `programs.csv` has **167 `funds_companies=no`**, **85 `yes`**, **43 `sometimes`**, **7 `unknown`** rows, but is not an exhaustive independent count of unique grant programs. The claim that **only 13 funders backed at least three U2 ventures** is correct (`investor_links.csv` with `universe=U2`). The section header expressly includes U1 science-topic ventures as well as U2 (line **366**), whereas the bottom-line figure of **97** and **13** concerns U2 alone; these are not interchangeable denominators. `ventures.csv` records `source_list=github_core` for **all 387 U1** and no science-topic membership column in the supplied data. Thus the U1-science-plus-U2 ranking (e.g. Kickstarter **14**) cannot be independently recreated exactly from these files without the earlier science-topic classification or an explicit key list.

**Correction.** Say “Kickstarter is the most frequent *individual crowd label*; venture firms are the most common **funder type** in U2.” Publish the U1-science key list, separate U2-only and expanded science/comparable tables, and stratify by hardware, instruments, scientific software, AI-for-science and DeSci; show **first cheques and leads**, not just name frequency. For an open physical-science founder, prioritize grant eligibility, prototype/manufacturing stage, present-day cheque size and equipment expertise rather than transplanting general COSS rankings.

### 8. Medium — independent audit supports incompleteness, but its percentages are historical and some discrepancies are aliases

**Evidence.** In `edison_audit_comparison.csv` (40 ventures), `ours=180`, `edison=296`, `both=154`: hence **154/180=85.56% (~86%)** and **154/296=52.03% (~52%)**, as `FUNDERS.md` line **589** says. There are **26 only-ours** and **142 only-Edison** name occurrences; eight original ventures had zero in “ours” but some in “edison” (rows **2, 4, 6, 9, 19, 20, 23, 26**). This is not a precision/recall gold standard: on the `radixark` row **39**, for example, the `only_ours` string **“ldvp”** and `only_edison` **“ldv partners”** may refer to one entity. `FUNDERS.md` line **592** says higher-confidence Edison findings were subsequently added (`xed`), so the same 40 keys now have **304 investor links** in `investor_links.csv`, not 180; the 86% and 52% describe a **pre-augmentation** snapshot, not current recall. The statement that the literature check found “the two missing” Indiegogo backers and Footprint Coalition (line **590**) is already stale: `investors.csv` row **1,304** explicitly includes **Indiegogo backers** (one Open Bionics link), and `FUNDERS.md` line **572** also names them.

**Correction.** Date and archive the pre-audit snapshot, normalize both audits' funder aliases and funding types, and re-evaluate unmatched names and missing rounds against the current table. Remove Indiegogo from the still-missing list; retain Footprint until added. Do not quote the 86% as a current or statistically valid accuracy estimate.

### 9. Medium — material missing investor and program examples, notably science publishing and experimental instruments

**Evidence.** `ventures.csv` contains **no PeerJ**, and `investors.csv` contains neither **SAGE** as a publisher-investor nor PeerJ funding from its backer O'Reilly AlphaTech Ventures (the latter has one *other* portfolio link, `investors.csv` row **645**). PeerJ's [own 9 July 2014 financing announcement](https://peerj.com/blog/post/91251985913/exciting-times-peerj-secures-next-round-of-funding-led-by-sage-and-oreilly/) names **SAGE** and **O'Reilly**, describes their capital as a new investment, and says **O'Reilly Media and OATV** supported the open-access publisher from inception [`peerj2014`]. Record verified corporate and venture backers under the actual investing legal entities without double counting O'Reilly Media/OATV. `programs.csv` (302 rows) contains no **Tool Foundry** or **Footprint Coalition** program. The [Tool Foundry](https://www.toolfoundry.org/) accelerator states it gave **$50,000 per selected team**, supported by **Moore Foundation and Schmidt Futures** [`toolfoundry2019`]; [Experiment's Low-Cost Tools for Science](https://experiment.com/grants/tools) lists Footprint Coalition among supporters and identifies funded *open-source* instrument projects [`experiment2026`]. Neither is proven to be a currently open corporate-equity opportunity, so list them as **historical/project-level** funding routes. OpenFlexure's [own funding ledger](https://openflexure.org/about/funding) identifies **UK Research and Innovation/Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, the Royal Society**, and other research and challenge-grant funders for a specific open microscope project [`openflexure2026`]; the Royal Society is missing from `programs.csv` and `investors.csv`, but OpenFlexure itself is a **project**, not necessarily an eligible venture. Astera's [2026 announcement](https://astera.org/astera-partnering-with-the-national-science-foundation/) describes up to **$20 million** in matched Astera support alongside **$380 million** of National Science Foundation support for a programmable-cloud-laboratories test bed [`astera2026`]; `programs.csv` includes Astera generally but not this targeted partnership. The existing `programs.csv` rows **2/27** give conflicting **$51.8 million for CZI cycles 1–5** versus **$47 million for cycles 1–6**, and rows **26/28** repeat the same **$20 million** Open Source for Science Fund commitment. Those are not additive budgets.

**Correction.** Add and source PeerJ/SAGE/OATV as a true for-profit venture-financing example; add Tool Foundry, Experiment/Footprint, Royal Society/OpenFlexure and Astera/NSF lab infrastructure as **different program categories**, with dated eligibility and whether money went to a business, university or project. Reconcile conflicting CZI totals against primary award reports, and collapse double-entered commitments. An open-lab founder needs a **program/eligibility map** as much as an equity-investor roll call; a past grant to a university is not evidence that the same funder would finance a company.

### 10. Medium — statements about direct company grants and “open-source theses” are too categorical

**Evidence.** `FUNDERS.md` lines **499–505** assert “Moore granted to Julia Computing and, for Numba and Dask, to Continuum Analytics.” The only cited evidence in the supplied dataset is **`programs.csv` rows 243–245**, with recipient field `companies` and $600,000, $1,057,443 and $700,000; the corresponding `ventures.csv` rows **408** Anaconda and **435** JuliaHub do **not** have Moore in `investor_links.csv`. JuliaHub's own `ventures.csv.notes` says “Moore Foundation/Intel supported Julia generally, **not tied to company**.” The Moore URLs in `programs.csv` could not be parsed beyond “Grant Detail” during this check, so I **cannot** verify the actual legal grantees or upgrade project support to corporate financing. The statement “26 funders ... state an open-source thesis in their own words” (`FUNDERS.md` lines **45–47**) equals **26 nonempty `investors.csv.stated_open_source_thesis` cells**, not 26 verified dedicated COSS investors. Examples: M12's quoted line in `FUNDERS.md` **180** concerns appetite from acquirers/public markets, not an explicit investment mandate; Zerodha (line **191**) describes support for free and open-source software rather than venture investing. Conversely `programs.csv` rows **156** Heavybit, **162** Crane and **189** OpenCapital.vc are labelled “open-source investment thesis” but not captured by that 26-row flag. `FUNDERS.md`'s “most are large generalists” is a subjective characterization, not a reproducible size measure.

**Correction.** Differentiate a dedicated open-source fund mandate, occasional favorable investor commentary, strategic open-source grantmaking and a direct corporate grant. Cite the actual recipient/payee and investment terms before calling a grant company financing. Provide a transparent criteria field and date for “states a thesis,” rather than one boolean constructed from heterogeneous quotes.

### 11. Medium — this delivery cannot independently substantiate every linked example, historical claim or program amount

**Evidence.** The supplied directory contains only `FUNDERS.md`, `PROTOCOL.md` and seven CSVs, not the listed `FUNDER_LIST.md`, `data/investor_aliases.csv`, `data/yc_open_source.csv`, original `edison/` audit/literature reports, science-topic membership, or charts (`FUNDERS.md` lines **1–19, 590, 596–670**). The write-up's `data/` links also do not match these top-level CSV paths in the supplied workspace. I independently checked the **380 numeric cells** in the principal rank/lead/early-round/thesis tables, **12 parent rollups** and **56 type-mix cells**; all **448** table-cell comparisons agreed with their referenced aggregated CSVs. The audit ledger contains **454 verified** comparisons including six other matched bottom-line tests, **one mismatch** (event count), and **88 additional recomputed measures**; exact matches may inherit errors from the common deal input. The owner classification “frozen before collection,” source-review correction of **99** names (68/16/10/5), hand review of **12** links (9/3), portfolio-page check **105/77/70/68**, YC directory **183/289**, earlier science-topic membership, and broad literature assertion **45/47** are **not independently verifiable from these files**. Many program budgets have inconsistent horizons, in-kind contributions or overlapping grant rounds; do not sum the `committed_usd` column indiscriminately.

**Correction.** Supply the versioned source artifacts, alias and type rules, science-topic key list, original audit snapshots and original citation pages alongside a corrected funder list. Label third-party spot checks as reported rather than independently repeated, and put the seven actual CSVs at the paths used by hyperlinks. Do not treat arithmetic agreement with the generated tables as external fact-checking.

## Claims I could verify, and what remains uncertain

| Claim | Recomputed evidence | Verdict |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| U1–U3 ventures / disclosed outside funding | `ventures.csv`: **387 + 97 + 156 = 640**; **231 + 72 + 145 = 448** `funding_found=yes` | **Verified as recorded**; 439/448 have named links, nine have funding with no named investor. |
| Distinct funders / one-venture funders / at least five | `investor_links.csv` U1–U3: **1,697 / 1,294 / 102** | **Verified as raw data**, sensitive to entity and scope fixes (Finding 6). |
| Top ten concentration | **291 / 3,137 = 9.28%** links; U1–U3 YC **60**, Accel **32**, a16z **32**, Sequoia **30** | **Verified as raw-data ranking**; no causal inference about a unique “club.” |
| Funding events | `deals.csv` U1–U3: **1,386 records**, **1,381 `counted=yes`**, **1,319** approximate four-field groups | **1,320 not verified**; genuine unique-round count requires reviewed event IDs. |
| Corporate parent counts | `investor_links.csv`: Alphabet **44**, Intel **24**, NVIDIA **22**, Microsoft **20**, Samsung **20**, Salesforce **19** | **Verified as table aggregations**; aliases/ownership boundaries still need review. |
| Specialty funds and angels | All-four-group OSS Capital **15**, Uncorrelated **14**, Bessemer **20**, GV **20**; Rauch **20** raw | **Verified as raw counts**; Rauch **19** after the six demonstrated venture-pair merges. |
| U2 repeat backers and grants | U2 **97** ventures; **13** funders on three or more; **17** government-grant and **8** philanthropy links | **Verified as tagged raw U2 data**, not exhaustive company-grant coverage. |
| U4 totals and top rows | **402** ventures, **306** `funding_found=yes`; YC **253** U4-only, **313** across U1–U4 | **Verified as raw data**; company aliases and nonprofit/non-open rows require correction. |
| Source checks and audit | **4,815/5,118=94.08%** fetchable text matches; 40-venture comparison **154/180=85.56%**, **154/296=52.03%** | **Verified arithmetic**, not independently validated investment accuracy or current audit performance. |
| Grants mostly not through companies | `programs.csv`: **167/302** labelled `funds_companies=no`, **85 yes, 43 sometimes, 7 unknown** | **Supported for listed rows**; rows overlap and coverage is selected. |
| Large generalists lead most observed rounds | U1–U3 **a16z, Accel, Insight 19** led ventures each, NEA/Sequoia **17**, Index **12**, Benchmark **13** | **Verified as source-table counting**, not lead-cheque sizes, present interest or investment returns. |

**Method and limits.** I reconstructed deal participants from `lead` and `investors` in `counted=yes` rows and verified they produce precisely the **4,178** published investor–venture links; all seven numeric `investors.csv` aggregation fields also match `investor_links.csv`. No source census, funding-return study, validity-weighted random sample of all open ventures, systematic worldwide grant search, or primary confirmation of every deal was possible. The independent audit is of 40 previously sampled ventures and has been partly incorporated into the dataset. Absence from this selected inventory does **not** establish a funder has never invested. A non-random corpus of notable COSS/AI companies (U3), a YC/Runa-heavy U4, and topic-selected U2 cannot estimate the size or investor mix of a general open-science market. Program grants, crowdfunding/backers, debt, strategic stakes and venture equity are different products and should not be read as interchangeable investor appetite.

## Primary web sources added for this review

The inline reference keys refer to full entries in [`review_support/references.bib`](review_support/references.bib): [`sapphire2014`](https://sapphireventures.com/press/sap-ventures-becomes-sapphire-ventures/), [`partech2022`](https://partechpartners.com/news/partech-40-years-empowering-tech), [`cloudera2021`](https://www.cloudera.com/about/news-and-blogs/press-releases/2021-06-01-cloudera-enters-into-definitive-agreement-to-be-acquired-by-clayton-dubilier-and-rice-and-kkr-for-5-point-3-billion-dollars.html), [`peerj2014`](https://peerj.com/blog/post/91251985913/exciting-times-peerj-secures-next-round-of-funding-led-by-sage-and-oreilly/), [`owid2026`](https://ourworldindata.org/funding), [`votingworks2026`](https://www.voting.works/about), [`openflexure2026`](https://openflexure.org/about/funding), [`toolfoundry2019`](https://www.toolfoundry.org/), [`experiment2026`](https://experiment.com/grants/tools) and [`astera2026`](https://astera.org/astera-partnering-with-the-national-science-foundation/). The Foundation's Moore grant-detail pages were not retrievable beyond a heading, so their amounts and legal recipients remain unresolved here.

## Discretionary analytical decisions

- I compared headline totals with **U1–U3 only**, but angel, studio, thesis and program claims against the **U1–U4** rows specified in each section; this avoids shifting denominators quietly.
- I counted one unique `(investor, venture key)` pair for rankings and expanded every named investor in a `counted=yes` deal for event-lead counts; I did **not** treat a shared source URL as proof that two event rows are identical.
- I used conservative, explicitly enumerated alias and transaction exclusions as **separate sensitivity checks**, not as estimates of the “true” fully corrected list, because further identities and round roles need human validation.
- I relied on the companies' or funders' own public pages for external examples where accessible and withheld conclusions about the Moore grants' direct corporate recipients when the relevant detail pages were unreadable.
'''
